questions.question: Explain the meaning of revolution as historians use it, and distinguish political from economic revolutions with two dated examples of each.
questions.expected_answer: A revolution is a fundamental change in how something is done or organised, so deep that life afterwards is very different; it may be sudden or take decades. Political revolutions change who holds power and how a country is governed, such as the American Revolution of 1775 to 1783, the French Revolution from 1789, and the Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804. Economic revolutions change how goods are produced and how people work and live, such as the agricultural revolution of the eighteenth century and the Industrial Revolution from about 1750.

questions.question: Describe the open-field system, three changes of the agricultural revolution, and the effects of enclosure on different groups.
questions.expected_answer: Under the open-field system, villages divided large fields into strips, families farmed scattered strips, one field lay fallow each year, and villagers had rights to common land. Changes: Jethro Tull's seed drill planted seeds in rows; the four-field rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover ended the fallow year and fed animals in winter; Robert Bakewell's selective breeding produced larger animals. Enclosure fenced fields and commons into private farms through Acts of Parliament. Landowners gained more productive farms and food production rose, but poorer villagers lost their strips and common rights; many became low-paid labourers or moved to towns, supplying workers for factories.

questions.question: Describe how the domestic system worked, give two advantages and two disadvantages for workers, and explain why it led to the invention of spinning machines.
questions.expected_answer: A merchant bought raw wool or cotton and put it out to village families, who carded and spun it into thread and wove it into cloth at home; the merchant collected the cloth, paid by the piece, and sold it. Advantages: the family worked together at home; they set their own hours and could farm at harvest. Disadvantages: pay was low and uncertain and the merchant held the power; cottages were cramped and work could be long and slow. One weaver needed the yarn of several spinners, so spinning was the bottleneck; machines that spun faster would be very profitable, so the first inventions attacked spinning.
